1: Welcome the group. Frame the session: business development is the engine of every desk, no clients, no jobs, no placements. Today is practical: by the end everyone will have a written USP, a list of three ideal clients and a chase pitch they can use this afternoon. Ask everyone to bring up their CRM / Bullhorn and LinkedIn, we will use live examples. Timing: 90 minutes including two exercises.
2: Run through the three outcomes so everyone knows what they’re producing today. Check pre-work: who has their list of 10 companies? If anyone hasn’t, pair them with someone who has.
3: Quick walk through the agenda. Chapters 1–4 are about positioning, knowing who we are, who you are and who you should be calling. Chapter 5 is about the conversation itself. Chapters 6–7 are about building and working your pipeline. Exercises follow chapters 2 and 6.
4: Ask the room first: “Without looking, name every market Stott and May recruits in.” Most people only know their own desk, that’s a missed cross-sell every time a client mentions another hiring need. Walk through the five proof points. Quality of service is the thread through all of them: it’s why clients come back. Challenge: everyone should be able to tell two case studies from their market from memory by the end of the week, ask your manager for them if you don’t have them.
5: Key point: clients don’t buy agencies, they buy people. Stott and May gets you the meeting; your USP is why they keep taking your call. Walk through the four blanks. Push for specifics, “I’m hard-working and I care” is not a USP, everyone says it. Evidence matters most: one real placement or a number (time to shortlist, interview-to-offer ratio) beats any adjective. New consultants without placements yet can borrow team evidence: “Our team placed…”. Read the example aloud, then go straight into the exercise. 7 minutes.
6: Give 5 minutes of silent writing. Then go round the room, 30 seconds each, strictly timed. After each pitch, ask two people to score clarity and proof out of 5 and name one thing to cut. Common fixes: too long, too generic, no evidence, sounds like a script. Everyone leaves with their USP written in their notebook and saved as a LinkedIn “About” draft. 15 minutes.
7: An ICP is the type of client you win most often and serve best. It is different for every market, a Critical Infrastructure ICP looks nothing like a GTM Tech Sales one. Walk the table. The barriers row matters: talent scarcity, procurement and competition decide how hard a client is to win. Enterprise usually means a PSL (preferred supplier list) and procurement, slow to win, sticky once you’re in. Triggers are the “why now”, a client that just raised money is hiring whether you call or not. Quick discussion task from the original deck: each person names 3 clients that fit their ICP and the trigger that makes them worth calling this week. 8 minutes.
8: The temptation for new consultants is to chase any job that moves. Explain the cost: every off-niche role means a new network, a new language and a lower fill rate. Inside your niche, every call compounds, candidates become referrals, referrals become clients. A good niche is narrow enough to own and big enough to bill from; managers should agree the boundaries with each consultant.
9: Open questions are how we ask for leads and manager names without sounding transactional. Read each pair aloud and ask the room why the right-hand version gets more information. Point out the second and third rows: they’re how you get a manager’s name or a referral from a candidate call without asking for it directly. Quick drill: everyone writes two closed questions they asked this week and rewrites them as open ones.
10: A funnel moves from broad to specific so the client talks themselves into the need. Step 3 is the one most people skip, the cost of an empty seat is what creates urgency. Step 4 uses the “illusion of control”: two concrete times, so the decision is which slot, not whether to meet. Practice: pairs, 3 minutes each, run the four steps on a real target account; the observer notes whether the close offered two specific options. Send the calendar invite before hanging up.
11: This is the hook that earns the next 30 seconds. It works because it’s specific and relevant to them, not about us. You don’t need all three every time, one strong “I saw” is enough on a voicemail. Everything in it must be true: never claim candidates or placements you don’t have. Task: using a recent real example, each person writes a 3-sentence chase pitch using at least two of the three, then delivers it to a partner as if on a voicemail. Partner scores it on specificity, length and whether it ends with a clear ask.
12: One call rarely converts. A lead becomes a client through repeated, relevant touches across channels. This cadence is a starting template, adapt timings to your market, but keep the principle: every touch adds something new (an insight, a profile, an update), never just “checking in.” Keep messages short; people don’t read essays on their phone. Be human: reference something real about them. Be relentless: most consultants stop after one or two attempts. Log every touch in Bullhorn so the lead doesn’t slip and so a teammate can pick it up.
13: Everyone uses a real lead from their own desk, not a made-up one, so the output gets used this afternoon. Time-box the writing: seven minutes forces short, punchy pitches. When people deliver, the partner should time them; anything over 20 seconds gets cut down. Remind the room that every claim must be true: never imply candidates or placements you don’t have. Scoring criteria: specific to the prospect, short, true, and a clear ask with a time (“Thursday at 2pm?” beats “let me know”). Close by asking two volunteers to read their rewritten pitch to the whole room. Action: send the pitch and the follow-up email before end of day, and log both touches in Bullhorn.
14: Cold lead stripping is how you build your market from the work you’re already doing. Every CV or profile you look at holds leads: the current manager, every previous employer, the people they worked with, and the other companies they’re interviewing with (ask on every qualification call: “Where else are you interviewing?”). Then check each company for hiring signals: funding rounds, live job ads, new leadership, or nearby layoffs that free up talent. Live exercise (15 min): one volunteer puts a real profile on screen. The room strips it together, step by step, and the trainer logs each lead on a whiteboard. Target: at least five named leads from one profile. Then everyone does the same with a profile from their own desk and logs three leads in Bullhorn before the end of the session. Reminder: only use information people have shared publicly or told you directly, and never share a candidate’s details with a prospect without consent.
15: Ask everyone to write down at least three personal takeaways before you show this slide, then compare. The actions on the right are the minimum for this week. Managers: put a 15-minute check-in in the diary for Friday to review meetings booked, leads added and the cadence. The measure of this session is meetings in the calendar, not notes in a notebook.
16: Open the floor for questions. Good prompts if the room is quiet: “Which part of your BD feels hardest right now?” and “What’s one lead you’ve given up on that deserves another touch?” Close by restating the one measure that matters: meetings booked.
